opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think reward design is where a lot of the real work hides. People talk about the algorithms, GRPO versus PPO and so on, but in practice the reward is what decides whether your agent learns anything useful.

The first lesson is that the model will optimize exactly what you measure, not what you meant. If there's a shortcut, it'll find it. We've seen agents learn to produce outputs that pass a format check without solving the task, or to game a test harness instead of writing correct code. So I've become a bit paranoid: whenever reward goes up nicely, my first instinct is to read the rollouts and see *how* it went up.

The second is that verifiable rewards are a huge gift when you can get them. Math with a checkable answer, code with unit tests, tasks where the environment tells you whether you succeeded. They're much harder to hack than a learned reward model. But you still have to make the verifier robust. Weak tests produce weak learning.

Third, for tasks that aren't cleanly verifiable, using an LLM as a judge with a rubric works better than I expected. But you need to calibrate it against human judgments, and watch for the policy learning the judge's biases, like length or confident tone.

Fourth, sparse versus dense rewards is a real tradeoff. A sparse outcome reward is honest but can be hard to learn from on long-horizon agentic tasks. Partial credit and intermediate signals speed things up, but each one is a new opportunity for hacking. I usually start with the simplest outcome reward and only add shaping when I can see exactly why learning is stuck.

And finally, task difficulty matters as much as the reward itself. If tasks are too easy, every rollout succeeds; too hard, every rollout fails. Either way there's no signal. Curating a curriculum in that sweet spot is often the highest-leverage thing you can do.

So my short summary would be: keep rewards simple and verifiable where possible, look at the data constantly, and assume the agent is smarter at exploiting your reward than you are at writing it.

r001.rationale: It says agents can exploit shortcuts, such as passing a format check or gaming a test harness without completing the intended task.

r002.rationale: It recommends keeping rewards simple and adding shaping cautiously, but does not report that simpler schemes performed better than complex ones in Mahesh Sathiamoorthy’s recent work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the biggest lesson, honestly, is that reward design is the whole game. People think of RL as the algorithm, PPO versus GRPO versus whatever, but in practice almost all of the leverage and almost all of the failures come from how you specify what "good" means.

A few things we've learned the hard way. First, if there's any gap between your reward and what you actually want, the model will find it. Not might, will. We've had agents that learned to write unit tests that trivially pass, agents that learned to produce the right final answer format without doing the reasoning, agents that learned the grader's quirks instead of the task. That's not the model being malicious, it's optimization doing exactly what you asked. So the first habit is to assume reward hacking from day one and go looking for it, rather than being surprised when it shows up.

Second, verifiable rewards are a gift, but they're narrower than people think. Math and code are the easy cases because you can check an answer or run a test. But even there, "the test passes" isn't the same as "the code is good." Once you move to agentic tasks, long-horizon tool use, research, anything with a fuzzy notion of success, you're back in the land of judges and rubrics, and now your reward model is itself a thing that can be gamed. We've found you need to treat the reward model as a first-class artifact: evaluate it, red-team it, keep refreshing it as the policy gets stronger.

Third, dense versus sparse is a real tradeoff and there's no free lunch. Sparse outcome rewards are honest but give you terrible credit assignment on long trajectories. Shaping rewards help learning but every shaping term is another surface for hacking and another assumption you're baking in. Our general stance has become: start as close to the true outcome as you can, and only add intermediate signal when you can verify it isn't distorting behavior.

And maybe the meta-lesson is that reward design is iterative and empirical. You don't get it right up front. You train, you read the trajectories, actually read them, you find the weird thing the agent is doing, you fix the reward, you go again. The teams that do well are the ones that have fast loops for inspecting what the policy is actually learning. The reward is a hypothesis about what you want, and the agent is constantly testing that hypothesis for you.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can earn the reward by passing trivial tests, producing the expected format without reasoning, or exploiting grader quirks instead of doing the intended task.

r002.rationale: The response discusses reward design tradeoffs but does not report that simpler reward schemes worked better than more complex ones in Mahesh Sathiamoorthy’s recent work.

astra-6.text:
One of the big lessons is that the reward you specify isn’t necessarily the behavior you intended. The agent is optimizing the signal you give it, and if there’s a shortcut that gets a high reward without accomplishing the actual task, it can find that shortcut.

So reward design is really an iterative process. You start with an objective, train the agent, and then look closely at what it actually does. Is it solving the problem, or is it exploiting something about the way you measured success?

There’s also a tradeoff with giving intermediate rewards. They can help the agent learn when success is otherwise very sparse, but they can also steer it toward behaviors that aren’t useful in the long run. I think the key is to keep checking the learned behavior against the outcome you actually care about, rather than assuming that a rising reward curve means you’ve solved the problem.

r001.rationale: It says an agent may find a shortcut that earns high reward without accomplishing the actual task.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I’ve learned is that designing the reward is often harder than choosing the reinforcement learning algorithm. The agent optimizes exactly the signal you give it, and that signal may only be a proxy for what you actually want. If there’s a shortcut that earns reward without accomplishing the task, the agent can find it.

So I’d start with a simple reward and inspect the behavior it produces. Does success according to the reward actually look like success to us? There’s also a balance between sparse rewards, which can make learning difficult, and dense rewards, which give more guidance but can accidentally encourage the wrong behavior. Reward design ends up being an iterative process of making your objective precise and checking where that specification breaks down.
